questions.q: What does end() return for a container in the STL's iterator convention?
options: An iterator to the last valid element
An iterator to one position past the last valid element
A null pointer
The total number of elements in the container
questions.explain: The half-open range convention means end() points one past the last valid element, which makes an empty range simply begin() == end().

questions.q: Why can std::sort(v.begin(), v.end()) work on both std::vector and std::deque without any container-specific code?
options: vector and deque are secretly the same type internally
std::sort is written purely in terms of iterator operations, and both containers' iterators support the random-access operations sort requires
std::sort converts every container to a vector before sorting
Only vector actually supports std::sort; deque silently does nothing
questions.explain: Algorithms like std::sort are written against iterator capabilities, not against a specific container type, so any container whose iterators meet the required category works.

questions.q: In `std::accumulate(prices.begin(), prices.end(), 0.0)`, what is the purpose of the third argument, 0.0?
options: It specifies how many elements to accumulate
It is the initial value the fold starts from, and its type should match the sum being computed
It is ignored by accumulate
It sets the precision of the result
questions.explain: accumulate folds the range starting from the given initial value; passing 0 instead of 0.0 for a double sum can cause the result to be computed as an integer and truncated.

questions.q: Why can't std::sort be called directly on a std::list's iterators?
options: std::list does not have iterators at all
std::sort only works on std::vector
std::list's iterators are only bidirectional, not random-access, and std::sort requires random-access iterators
std::list elements cannot be compared
questions.explain: std::sort needs random-access iterators (constant-time jumps by n). std::list's iterators are only bidirectional, so std::list instead provides its own sort() member function.

questions.q: A range-based for loop like `for (const auto& p : prices)` is syntactic sugar for what underlying pattern?
options: A recursive function call over the container
Calling prices.size() repeatedly and indexing each time
An iterator-based loop using begin() and end() with ++ to advance
A call to std::accumulate
questions.explain: The range-based for loop is compiler-generated iterator traversal: it calls begin()/end() and dereferences/increments the iterator each pass.
